subject: Expected density from Temp Em model

messages.author: 0886a511cd5fa3ed
messages.subject: Expected density from Temp Em model
parts:
Hi,
I am working from the temporary emigration examples from the recent workshop at Patuxent. I would like to calculate expected density, however when I run the sample code below the value returned is NA. 
Any thoughts on why density values are not returned? 
Thanks!!

# my model
(fm2ClassGPC<-gpcount(~EM1, ~BC, ~Obs+Time, clra.umf, mixture="NB", K = 20))

# Compute expected density in sampled area
D.fn <- function(fm) {
    E.M <- predict(fm, type="lambda")[,1]
    E.phi <- predict(fm, type="phi")[,1]
    plot.area <- pi*150^2 / 1e4 # hectares # 150 m radius counts
    nSites <- length(E.M)
    E.D <- sum(E.M * E.phi) / (plot.area*nSites)
    return(E.D)
}
D.fn(fm2ClassGPC) #  birds/hectare

messages.author: df74d6fccec2ff7e
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Expected density from Temp Em model
parts:
Hi Kathi,

predict(fm, type="state") returns "lambda" the expected value of "super-population size" (M) at each plot. 
In our Ecology paper, we focused on random temporary emigration such that M equals the total number of individuals that use the plot during the season. In that case, "phi" is the probability that an individual is present (on the plot) during a primary period, and the expected value of density is 

E[D] = E[N]/A = (lambda*phi)/A. 

where N the number of individuals on the plot during a primary period, and A is plot area. This model can be used to model processes other than temporary emigration, in which case the parameters (lambda and phi) will have different interpretations. 

If the estimates of M seem too high, it is probably because the estimates of p and/or phi are very low.

Richard
